Triggers.value: Beginning to feel detached or unreal

Threat.value: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger

Memory.value: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.

Negative Appraisals.value: I have permanently changed for the worse
I have to be on guard all the time
I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

issues.explanation: The trigger set mixes a socially evaluative trigger ('being seen') with nonspecific discomfort/detachment, while the threat items center on danger from sudden sounds, home intrusion, and interpersonal harm. For a combat trauma profile, 'being seen' is not impossible, but here it is poorly linked to the stated threat pattern and stands out as the one trigger not plausibly connected to the strong Triggers→Threat and Triggers→Negative Appraisals edges.

issues.item: Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: Within Threat, hypervigilance to loud sounds and watching others for danger fit a combat-related threat profile, but specifically monitoring for someone entering the home implies a domestic intrusion threat context that is not supported by the triggers, memory, or appraisals. It pulls the profile toward a different trauma context and weakens cross-node coherence.

vignette: At forty-six, Marcus had spent nearly two decades running quiet trails through the Pacific Northwest canopy as a park ranger, yet his mind remained stationed in a foreign valley where the air always tasted of burnt rubber and cordite. During a routine convoy patrol in combat, a sudden ambush had shattered his unit’s formation. Enemy helicopters had thumped overhead, their downdraft kicking up choking dust as automatic fire erupted from the ridgeline. Marcus remembered freezing, his boots rooted to the ground while his squad moved ahead of him, a moment of inaction he still replayed in crystal detail. He could still taste the metallic grit of the air and smell the acrid, chemical scent of spent propellant. The memory never faded to background noise; it pressed against his present consciousness with a clarity that made ordinary moments feel flat by comparison. When a distant agricultural plane drifted over the park years later, its engine pitch mimicking a rotor, Marcus felt that familiar hollow detachment in his chest, his body growing stiff and uncomfortable. That jolt instantly threw him into a state of hyperalertness; his head snapped up, eyes scanning the treeline and trail for any sign of movement, while he watched the small group of hikers nearby for any gesture that might signal hostility. Because he lived in this state of perceived danger, his nervous system stayed primed, making his threat appraisal actively pull his attention back toward the valley where the helicopters came down. The constant scanning and watching for hidden threats, in turn, sharpened his sensitivity to every distant aircraft and sudden noise, turning mild environmental cues into urgent alarms that demanded immediate assessment. This hypervigilant posture cemented his conviction that he was permanently damaged for the worse. The recurrence of that hollow detachment and physical discomfort served as daily proof to him that he was irrevocably changed, directly feeding his negative appraisals. Because he was certain he carried an unfixable burden of inaction guilt, the memories stopped fading and instead pressed forward, becoming more real and vivid than his actual surroundings. His conviction that he had to remain on guard at all times made him hyper-sensitive to his own discomfort and dissociative feelings, turning them into urgent alerts rather than passing sensations. Conversely, when those vivid, olfactory-laden memories of the ambush invaded his mind, they directly reinforced his negative self-view; the clearer the recall, the more certain he became that his emotional numbness was permanent. The relentless threat monitoring and constant reading of others as hostile drained his resilience, directly feeding his conviction that he was broken and would never forgive himself. Over months, this narrow loop shrank his world. He stopped taking long routes through dense brush, avoiding the quiet valleys that once brought him peace. His wife noticed the distance in his eyes, how he would sit at the dinner table straining his ears for ceiling noises that weren’t there. It was the shrinking of his own life that finally pushed him to seek care. The relentless vigilance had left him exhausted, and the dissociative feelings during solo patrols were becoming frequent enough that he feared he would miss a visitor in distress. He came to the clinic hoping to untangle the knot of guilt that kept him braced for impact, desperate to reclaim the ability to simply walk a trail without his mind already back in the dust. What frightened him most was that the steady, grounded man he used to be might never return, but what he hoped for was simply a chance to finally lay down the watch.
